quests.hint: 'They' here refers back to 'a good leader', used for a general, gender-neutral subject.
quests.explanation: 'They' is commonly used as a singular, gender-neutral pronoun in modern English, even for a single unspecified person like 'a good leader'. This usage is now fully standard.
quests.textToSpeak: A good leader listens more than they speak in meetings.
quests.correctAnswer: A good leader listens more than they speak in meetings.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'They' here refers back to 'a good leader', used for a general, gender-neutral subject.

quests.hint: 'Alone' at the end of the sentence adds emphasis to 'technical skill'.
quests.explanation: Placing 'alone' after a noun stresses that something by itself isn't enough. This word order adds emphasis without needing extra words like 'only' or 'just'.
quests.textToSpeak: Effective communication is often more important than technical skill alone.
quests.correctAnswer: Effective communication is often more important than technical skill alone.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Alone' at the end of the sentence adds emphasis to 'technical skill'.

quests.hint: 'Giving credit' as the subject takes the singular verb 'builds'.
quests.explanation: 'Give credit to someone' means to publicly acknowledge their contribution or effort. This gerund-subject pattern, seen throughout this course, continues to take a singular verb.
quests.textToSpeak: Giving credit to your team builds long-term loyalty and trust.
quests.correctAnswer: Giving credit to your team builds long-term loyalty and trust.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Giving credit' as the subject takes the singular verb 'builds'.

quests.hint: 'Realise' uses the British spelling with an 's', not a 'z'.
quests.explanation: 'Realise' (British) and 'realize' (American) are both correct, differing only by spelling convention. 'Than most users realise' shows a gap between reality and common awareness.
quests.textToSpeak: Companies collect more personal data than most users realise.
quests.correctAnswer: Companies collect more personal data than most users realise.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Realise' uses the British spelling with an 's', not a 'z'.

quests.hint: 'Worth checking' is followed by the -ing form, not the infinitive.
quests.explanation: 'It's worth doing something' is a useful structure for recommending a helpful action. 'Every few months' describes a repeated but infrequent routine.
quests.textToSpeak: It's worth checking your privacy settings every few months.
quests.correctAnswer: It's worth checking your privacy settings every few months.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Worth checking' is followed by the -ing form, not the infinitive.

quests.hint: 'Adverts' is the British shortened form of 'advertisements'.
quests.explanation: 'Advert' is the common British short form of 'advertisement', while American English typically shortens it to 'ad'. 'Depending on your view' shows the outcome varies by opinion.
quests.textToSpeak: Targeted adverts can feel useful or unsettling, depending on your view.
quests.correctAnswer: Targeted adverts can feel useful or unsettling, depending on your view.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Adverts' is the British shortened form of 'advertisements'.

quests.hint: 'Choosing to walk' as the subject takes the singular verb 'is'.
quests.explanation: 'Small but meaningful' pairs two contrasting qualities using 'but', showing something modest can still matter. The gerund subject again takes a singular verb.
quests.textToSpeak: Choosing to walk instead of drive is a small but meaningful habit.
quests.correctAnswer: Choosing to walk instead of drive is a small but meaningful habit.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Choosing to walk' as the subject takes the singular verb 'is'.

quests.hint: Two gerund phrases joined by 'and' still count as one subject here.
quests.explanation: When two gerund phrases are joined by 'and' and treated as a single combined idea, the verb can stay singular, as here with 'reduces'. This shows just how flexible gerund subjects can be.
quests.textToSpeak: Buying less and repairing more reduces the waste we create.
quests.correctAnswer: Buying less and repairing more reduces the waste we create.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] Two gerund phrases joined by 'and' still count as one subject here.

quests.hint: 'Add up to' means the small things combine into something bigger.
quests.explanation: 'Add up to' describes how small, individual actions combine into a larger total effect. 'Collective' means shared by a whole group, useful vocabulary for talking about society.
quests.textToSpeak: Every household's choices add up to a larger collective impact.
quests.correctAnswer: Every household's choices add up to a larger collective impact.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Add up to' means the small things combine into something bigger.

quests.hint: 'Used to' describes a repeated past habit that has now stopped.
quests.explanation: 'Used to' describes past habits or states no longer true today. It's followed by the base verb, and is one of the clearest ways to talk about how life used to be different.
quests.textToSpeak: My parents used to argue about money when I was young.
quests.correctAnswer: My parents used to argue about money when I was young.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Used to' describes a repeated past habit that has now stopped.

quests.hint: 'Would' here describes a repeated past action, like 'used to'.
quests.explanation: 'Would' can describe repeated past actions, similar to 'used to', though it can't be used for past states like 'I would be tall'. It works best for describing habitual actions and events.
quests.textToSpeak: We would spend every summer at my grandparents' house.
quests.correctAnswer: We would spend every summer at my grandparents' house.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Would' here describes a repeated past action, like 'used to'.

quests.hint: 'Always used to' combines a frequency word with the past habit structure.
quests.explanation: Adding 'always' to 'used to' emphasises just how consistent a past habit or feeling was. 'A bit chaotic' softens the description slightly compared to just 'chaotic'.
quests.textToSpeak: Family gatherings always used to feel a bit chaotic.
quests.correctAnswer: Family gatherings always used to feel a bit chaotic.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Always used to' combines a frequency word with the past habit structure.

quests.hint: 'Should have' expresses a regret about something that didn't happen.
quests.explanation: 'Should have' plus a past participle expresses criticism or regret about a past action that didn't happen. This is a very common structure for expressing mild frustration politely.
quests.textToSpeak: You should have told me the meeting had been moved.
quests.correctAnswer: You should have told me the meeting had been moved.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Should have' expresses a regret about something that didn't happen.

quests.hint: 'Might have' offers a possible explanation for a past event.
quests.explanation: 'Might have' plus a past participle expresses uncertainty about something that possibly happened in the past. It's a gentle way to offer an alternative explanation without blaming anyone.
quests.textToSpeak: She might have misunderstood what you meant by that.
quests.correctAnswer: She might have misunderstood what you meant by that.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Might have' offers a possible explanation for a past event.

quests.hint: 'Could have' here suggests they had the ability but didn't use it.
quests.explanation: 'Could have' plus a past participle suggests an unused past possibility, often implying mild criticism. 'Before making the change' explains exactly when the warning should have happened.
quests.textToSpeak: They could have warned us before making the change.
quests.correctAnswer: They could have warned us before making the change.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Could have' here suggests they had the ability but didn't use it.

quests.hint: 'Honestly' at the start signals a frank, sincere opinion is coming.
quests.explanation: 'Honestly' at the beginning of a sentence prepares the listener for a direct, sincere opinion. 'Entirely' softens the criticism slightly compared to a blunt 'not realistic'.
quests.textToSpeak: Honestly, I'm not sure this plan is entirely realistic.
quests.correctAnswer: Honestly, I'm not sure this plan is entirely realistic.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Honestly' at the start signals a frank, sincere opinion is coming.

quests.hint: 'To be fair' introduces a balanced, generous perspective.
quests.explanation: 'To be fair' signals that the speaker is trying to be balanced, even while making a point. 'Under pressure' describes working in a stressful or demanding situation.
quests.textToSpeak: To be fair, the team did their best under pressure.
quests.correctAnswer: To be fair, the team did their best under pressure.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'To be fair' introduces a balanced, generous perspective.

quests.hint: 'As far as I know' limits the certainty of the claim that follows.
quests.explanation: 'As far as I know' shows the speaker's knowledge might be incomplete, adding a layer of honesty. 'Still on the table' is an idiom meaning an offer or option remains available.
quests.textToSpeak: As far as I know, the offer is still on the table.
quests.correctAnswer: As far as I know, the offer is still on the table.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'As far as I know' limits the certainty of the claim that follows.

quests.hint: 'An arm and a leg' is an idiom meaning a very high price.
quests.explanation: 'Cost an arm and a leg' is a common idiom meaning something is extremely expensive. Idioms like this add colour and humour to everyday conversation.
quests.textToSpeak: It costs an arm and a leg to fly during the holidays.
quests.correctAnswer: It costs an arm and a leg to fly during the holidays.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'An arm and a leg' is an idiom meaning a very high price.

quests.hint: 'Break the ice' means to ease tension at the start of a meeting.
quests.explanation: 'Break the ice' is an idiom meaning to relieve initial awkwardness or tension between people. It's especially useful vocabulary for talking about first meetings or interviews.
quests.textToSpeak: We need to break the ice before the interview starts.
quests.correctAnswer: We need to break the ice before the interview starts.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Break the ice' means to ease tension at the start of a meeting.

quests.hint: 'Jump to conclusions' means judging something too quickly.
quests.explanation: 'Jump to conclusions' means to make a judgement before having all the facts. This idiom is a useful reminder to stay open-minded in discussions and disagreements.
quests.textToSpeak: Let's not jump to conclusions before hearing the full story.
quests.correctAnswer: Let's not jump to conclusions before hearing the full story.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Jump to conclusions' means judging something too quickly.

quests.hint: 'Dragged on' suggests something continued for an unpleasantly long time.
quests.explanation: 'Drag on' describes something continuing longer than wanted or expected, often with a tone of mild frustration. 'Far longer than' strengthens the comparison beyond a simple 'longer than'.
quests.textToSpeak: The negotiations dragged on far longer than anyone expected.
quests.correctAnswer: The negotiations dragged on far longer than anyone expected.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Dragged on' suggests something continued for an unpleasantly long time.

quests.hint: 'Reached a compromise' is the standard phrase for successful negotiation.
quests.explanation: 'Reach a compromise' is a fixed collocation describing the successful end of a disagreement, where both sides give a little. 'Eventually' shows this took time to achieve.
quests.textToSpeak: Both sides eventually reached a compromise everyone could accept.
quests.correctAnswer: Both sides eventually reached a compromise everyone could accept.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Reached a compromise' is the standard phrase for successful negotiation.

quests.hint: 'It's rare for... to...' introduces an unusual situation.
quests.explanation: 'It's rare for X to happen' is a useful structure for commenting on unusual events. In business, 'close a deal' means to finalise an agreement successfully.
quests.textToSpeak: It's rare for a deal like this to close so quickly.
quests.correctAnswer: It's rare for a deal like this to close so quickly.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'It's rare for... to...' introduces an unusual situation.

quests.hint: 'Pass down' means to give something to the next generation.
quests.explanation: 'Pass down' describes something given from older to younger generations, like traditions, stories, or possessions. 'Shape' here means to strongly influence, a figurative use seen earlier in this course.
quests.textToSpeak: Grandparents often pass down traditions that shape a family's identity.
quests.correctAnswer: Grandparents often pass down traditions that shape a family's identity.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Pass down' means to give something to the next generation.

quests.hint: 'Once' here means 'after', introducing a change following an event.
quests.explanation: 'Once' meaning 'after' introduces a turning point that leads to change. 'Sibling' is a formal, neutral word for a brother or sister.
quests.textToSpeak: Sibling relationships can shift a lot once everyone leaves home.
quests.correctAnswer: Sibling relationships can shift a lot once everyone leaves home.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Once' here means 'after', introducing a change following an event.

quests.hint: 'Navigate' here means to manage carefully, not to find your way by map.
quests.explanation: 'Navigate' is often used figuratively to mean carefully managing a complicated situation. 'Blended family' describes a family formed when parents with children from previous relationships join together.
quests.textToSpeak: Blended families face unique challenges that take time to navigate.
quests.correctAnswer: Blended families face unique challenges that take time to navigate.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Navigate' here means to manage carefully, not to find your way by map.

quests.hint: 'By the time' introduces a deadline that a past event happened before.
quests.explanation: 'By the time' plus the past perfect shows one event was already completed before another happened. This structure is essential for describing the order of past events clearly.
quests.textToSpeak: By the time we arrived, the shop had already closed.
quests.correctAnswer: By the time we arrived, the shop had already closed.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'By the time' introduces a deadline that a past event happened before.

quests.hint: 'Will have finished' is the future perfect — an action completed before a future point.
quests.explanation: The future perfect, 'will have finished', describes an action that will be completed before a specific point in the future. 'By next year' sets that future deadline.
quests.textToSpeak: By next year, she'll have finished her medical training.
quests.correctAnswer: By next year, she'll have finished her medical training.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Will have finished' is the future perfect — an action completed before a future point.

quests.hint: This long sentence uses the same future perfect pattern — keep a steady pace throughout.
quests.explanation: This sentence reinforces the future perfect structure, useful for describing progress and outcomes by a certain point. 'The basics of' introduces the fundamental parts of any skill or subject.
quests.textToSpeak: By the end of the course, you'll have learned the basics of coding.
quests.correctAnswer: By the end of the course, you'll have learned the basics of coding.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] This long sentence uses the same future perfect pattern — keep a steady pace throughout.
